extra_quotes: Light from up to three tunable lasers (1530–1610 nm) is combined in fiber; a fraction is monitored on an optical spectrum analyzer. A function generator applies the sinusoidal bias between 3 and 10 V. The photodiode is terminated in 100 Ω; a bias tee separates the DC photocurrent, recorded directly, from the AC component, which is amplified by a low-noise amplifier (1 kHz–1.8 GHz) and digitized by an oscilloscope as 8000 samples over one bias period, triggered by the function generator.

Each dark-subtracted waveform is compressed onto 10–20 principal components, computed from calibration waveforms only, and a fully connected neural network maps them, together with the DC photocurrent, to the line wavelengths; a second network classifies the power of each line.

Consistent with the line coupling of Sec. 4.2, a linear inversion with a dictionary of measured single-line waveforms recovers single lines but not multi-line spectra (Table 3), confirming that the coupled response must be learned from calibration spectra of the same kind as those to be measured.
On a new day the accuracy is set by slow day-to-day drift rather than by noise

for three lines, recorded on fewer days, it remains above 1 nm, and calibration over more days, together with temperature stabilization of the photodiode and monitoring of the bias waveform, is the direct route to improving it.
